newsitem.title: BELGIUM: CAP changes to go to Council after committee fails to agree.
newsitem.headline: CAP changes to go to Council after committee fails to agree.

text.p: European Union agriculture experts failed at a two-day meeting on Monday and Tuesday to agree a number of key changes to EU agriculture policy which are now expected to be put on the agenda of the December farm Council.
Talks will continue next week on changing the system of penalties for overshooting national planting area limits, an EU official said on Wednesday.
"National experts meeting in the EU's special agriculture committee held a long discussion on Monday and Tuesday but it came to nothing," the official said.
Germany has proposed that the system of penalising farmers for overplanting base areas should be aimed at those who are responsible for the overshoot.
The German case is that its individual states should be penalised rather than have all of them share the burden of a one per cent cut in EU aid for every one per cent overshoot.
"The problem is that several member states have ideas of their own which amount to letting farmers off the penalty altogether," the official said.
According to a British diplomat fears were expressed in the committee that some of the proposed changes would lead to overproduction.
"This will come up again at next week's special agriculture committee and may go to the December meeting of farm ministers," the diplomat said.
The committee was also split on a special tariff quota for the import of animals from eastern European countries.
"There was a brief discussion on Tuesday but no agreement could be reached. It will now go on the Irish Presidency's list for the December farm Council," the official said.
The proposal to allow imports of eastern European farm animals at a reduced tariff has run into difficulty because of the EU's GATT commitments.
"Under the GATT agreement any relaxation of tariffs for eastern Europe must be available to every GATT partner and this has brought out the protectionists," the official said.
Disputes over a change to the European Union's geographic denomination rules will also go to farm ministers.
"The change in the rules would allow manufacturers of foods caught in the geographic denominations list a period of grace before they have to change their product descriptions," the official said.
The committee split between north and south on this issue which, for example, would restrict the description of a cheese not made in the area where the cheese came from originally.
